title: A color scientist who’s never seen red poses a puzzle about the mind
body: In 1982 philosopher Frank Jackson imagined Mary, a brilliant scientist who has learned every physical fact about color and vision while living in a black-and-white room. One day she steps out and sees a ripe tomato. If she learns something new, namely what seeing red is like, then not every fact is a physical fact, and physicalism, the view that everything is physical, looks incomplete.

slides.heading: The setup
slides.text: Mary knows the wavelengths, the retina, the neurons and every word we use about color. She has simply never experienced a color herself.

slides.heading: The question
slides.text: When she first sees red, does she learn something? Jackson called the ‘irresistible conclusion’ that there are more properties than physicalists talk about.

slides.heading: The replies
slides.text: Some say she gains new abilities, like imagining red, not new facts. Daniel Dennett argued that a truly all-knowing Mary would not be surprised at all.

slides.prompt: What did Frank Jackson himself eventually make of his own argument?
slides.answer: He rejected it and became a physicalist
slides.detail: The argument remains one of the most debated ideas in philosophy of mind, even though its author changed his mind.

slides.heading: The twist
slides.text: Jackson himself later became a physicalist and rejected his own argument, yet it remains one of the most debated ideas in philosophy of mind.
